nameStory: The 'glandular' in this mussel's name refers to the small, bump-like structures scattered across its shell surface that look remarkably like tiny glands or pores. The 'bean' part comes from its distinctly kidney bean or lima bean shape when viewed from the side. Early naturalists thought these shell bumps might actually secrete something, though they're simply part of the shell's unique texture.
description: The Glandular Bean Mussel is a small, freshwater bivalve with a distinctly bean-shaped shell that's quite different from the typical teardrop shape of most mussels. These compact mollusks typically reach only 1-2 inches in length, making them one of the smaller mussel species in New England waters. Their shells are marked by characteristic raised bumps or nodules that give them a distinctly textured, almost warty appearance. Like other mussels, they filter feed by drawing water through their bodies and straining out tiny particles of food.

idTips.label: Shell shape
idTips.description: Distinctly kidney bean or lima bean shaped when viewed from the side, much rounder and less elongated than typical mussels

idTips.label: Surface texture
idTips.description: Shell feels noticeably bumpy with small, raised nodules scattered across the surface like tiny pebbles glued on

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Small and compact, typically 1-2 inches long, fitting easily in the palm of your hand

idTips.label: Shell color
idTips.description: Dark brown to blackish exterior, often with lighter brown bands; interior is typically pearly white or pale yellow

idTips.label: Shell thickness
idTips.description: Feels surprisingly heavy and solid for its size, with thick shell walls that resist gentle pressure

habitat: Found in clean, flowing rivers and larger streams with rocky or gravelly bottoms throughout New England's watersheds. They prefer areas with moderate to swift current where they can anchor themselves between rocks and receive a steady flow of food particles. Look for them partially buried in coarse sand and gravel substrates in water depths of 1-6 feet.

seasonality.spring: Most active as water temperatures rise and food becomes more abundant. This is when they're most likely to be filter feeding actively and easiest to spot.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity period when shells are often partially open for feeding. Low water levels may expose more individuals in shallow areas.
seasonality.fall: Still active but beginning to prepare for winter dormancy. Shells may be more tightly closed as temperatures drop.
seasonality.winter: Largely dormant under ice, with shells clamped shut. Very difficult to find or identify during this season.

funFact: Despite their small size, a single Glandular Bean Mussel can filter up to 10 gallons of water per day, making them incredibly efficient natural water purifiers that can help keep entire stream systems clean!
confusionNotes: Most commonly confused with young Eastern Elliptio mussels, but the bean-like shape and bumpy texture are dead giveaways. Remember: if it looks like a kidney bean with goosebumps, you've found a Glandular Bean Mussel!
contextualKnowledge: The scientific name 'Solamen' means 'comfort' or 'solace' in Latin, possibly referring to their role as indicators of healthy, clean waterways. Finding these mussels is actually comforting news for stream health, as they're quite sensitive to pollution.
compareHints: As the only member of the Solamen genus in New England, this species is most easily compared to other small freshwater mussels in the region. Unlike the more common Eastern Elliptio or Eastern Pearlshell mussels, Glandular Bean Mussels have that distinctive rounded, bean-like profile and uniquely bumpy shell texture. Most other regional mussels have smooth or ridged shells with more elongated, teardrop shapes.
